title: Exercise 7A · Q10(c)
summary: Find BE, solve for e in ΔADE, then find f in ΔBDC.
alt: Exercise 7A · Q10(c): In the figure, the diagonals AC and BE meet at D at right angles, ∠ABE = 90°, AB = 22 cm, AE = 32 cm, AD = 27 cm, BC = 5e, DE = 4e and CD = f. Find the values of e and f.

hyp.label: Hypotenuse
hyp.text: The side opposite the right angle. It is always the longest side.

legA.label: Shorter side 1
legA.text: One of the two sides that meet at the right angle.

legB.label: Shorter side 2
legB.text: The other side that meets at the right angle.

steps.title: The question
steps.narration: In the figure (**not drawn to scale**), the diagonals **AC** and **BE** meet at **D** at right angles. **∠ABE = 90°**. **AB = 22 cm**, **AE = 32 cm**, **AD = 27 cm**, **BC = 5e**, **DE = 4e** and **CD = f**. We have to find **e** and **f**.

steps.title: Right angle and theorem
steps.narration: In ΔABE, **∠B = 90°**, so the **hypotenuse** is the side opposite it: **AE**. The other two sides meet at the right angle. **Pythagoras' theorem**: the square on the hypotenuse equals the sum of the squares on the other two sides. We want a shorter side, so subtract.\[\begin{aligned}\role{hyp}{AE^2} &= \role{legA}{AB^2} + \role{legB}{BE^2} \\ \role{legB}{BE^2} &= \role{hyp}{AE^2} - \role{legA}{AB^2}\end{aligned}\]

steps.title: Substitute and subtract
steps.narration: Put in the lengths, square them and subtract.\[\begin{aligned}\role{hyp}{AE^2} &= \role{legA}{AB^2} + \role{legB}{BE^2} \\ \role{legB}{BE^2} &= \role{hyp}{AE^2} - \role{legA}{AB^2} \\ &= \role{hyp}{32^2} - \role{legA}{22^2} \\ &= \role{hyp}{1024} - \role{legA}{484} \\ &= \role{legB}{540}\end{aligned}\]

steps.title: Square root
steps.narration: 540 is not a perfect square. Use a calculator and keep 4 significant figures — we need this value again.\[\begin{aligned}\role{hyp}{AE^2} &= \role{legA}{AB^2} + \role{legB}{BE^2} \\ \role{legB}{BE^2} &= \role{hyp}{AE^2} - \role{legA}{AB^2} \\ &= \role{hyp}{32^2} - \role{legA}{22^2} \\ &= \role{hyp}{1024} - \role{legA}{484} \\ &= \role{legB}{540} \\ \role{legB}{BE} &= \sqrt{540} = 23.24\ \text{cm}\end{aligned}\]

steps.title: Equation for e
steps.narration: In **ΔADE**, **∠D = 90°** (the diagonals meet at right angles), so **AE** is the hypotenuse. Use Pythagoras' theorem, with **DE = 4e**.\[\begin{aligned}\role{hyp}{AE^2} &= \role{legA}{AD^2} + \role{legB}{DE^2}\end{aligned}\]

steps.title: Substitute the lengths
steps.narration: Replace each side by its length.\[\begin{aligned}\role{hyp}{AE^2} &= \role{legA}{AD^2} + \role{legB}{DE^2} \\ \role{hyp}{32^2} &= \role{legA}{27^2} + \role{legB}{(4e)^2} \\ \role{hyp}{1024} &= \role{legA}{729} + \role{legB}{16e^2}\end{aligned}\]

steps.title: Solve for e²
steps.narration: Move 729 across, then divide by 16.\[\begin{aligned}\role{hyp}{AE^2} &= \role{legA}{AD^2} + \role{legB}{DE^2} \\ \role{hyp}{32^2} &= \role{legA}{27^2} + \role{legB}{(4e)^2} \\ \role{hyp}{1024} &= \role{legA}{729} + \role{legB}{16e^2} \\ 16e^2 &= 1024 - 729 = 295 \\ e^2 &= \frac{295}{16}\end{aligned}\]

steps.title: Find e
steps.narration: Take the positive square root.\[\begin{aligned}\role{hyp}{AE^2} &= \role{legA}{AD^2} + \role{legB}{DE^2} \\ \role{hyp}{32^2} &= \role{legA}{27^2} + \role{legB}{(4e)^2} \\ \role{hyp}{1024} &= \role{legA}{729} + \role{legB}{16e^2} \\ 16e^2 &= 1024 - 729 = 295 \\ e^2 &= \frac{295}{16} \\ e &= \frac{\sqrt{295}}{4} = \role{ans}{4.29\ \text{cm}}\ \text{(3 s.f.)}\end{aligned}\]

steps.title: Find BD
steps.narration: Now **DE = 4e** and **BD = BE − DE**. Keep the digits **e = 4.294**.\[\begin{aligned}DE &= 4e = 4 \times 4.294 = 17.18\ \text{cm} \\ BD &= BE - DE \\ &= 23.24 - 17.18 \\ &= 6.06\ \text{cm}\end{aligned}\]

steps.title: Right angle and theorem
steps.narration: In ΔBDC, **∠D = 90°**, so the **hypotenuse** is the side opposite it: **BC**. The other two sides meet at the right angle. **Pythagoras' theorem**: the square on the hypotenuse equals the sum of the squares on the other two sides. We want a shorter side, so subtract.\[\begin{aligned}\role{hyp}{BC^2} &= \role{legA}{BD^2} + \role{legB}{CD^2} \\ \role{legB}{CD^2} &= \role{hyp}{BC^2} - \role{legA}{BD^2}\end{aligned}\]

steps.title: Substitute and subtract
steps.narration: Put in the lengths, square them and subtract.\[\begin{aligned}\role{hyp}{BC^2} &= \role{legA}{BD^2} + \role{legB}{CD^2} \\ \role{legB}{CD^2} &= \role{hyp}{BC^2} - \role{legA}{BD^2} \\ &= \role{hyp}{21.47^2} - \role{legA}{6.06^2} \\ &= \role{hyp}{460.96} - \role{legA}{36.72} \\ &= \role{legB}{424.24}\end{aligned}\]

steps.title: Square root
steps.narration: 424.24 is not a perfect square, so use a calculator and round to 3 significant figures.\[\begin{aligned}\role{hyp}{BC^2} &= \role{legA}{BD^2} + \role{legB}{CD^2} \\ \role{legB}{CD^2} &= \role{hyp}{BC^2} - \role{legA}{BD^2} \\ &= \role{hyp}{21.47^2} - \role{legA}{6.06^2} \\ &= \role{hyp}{460.96} - \role{legA}{36.72} \\ &= \role{legB}{424.24} \\ \role{legB}{CD} &= \sqrt{424.24} = \role{ans}{20.6\ \text{cm}}\end{aligned}\]

formulas.title: Pythagoras' theorem
formulas.text: In a right-angled triangle, the square on the hypotenuse equals the sum of the squares on the other two sides.

formulas.title: Finding the hypotenuse
formulas.text: Add the two squares, then take the square root.

formulas.title: Finding a shorter side
formulas.text: Subtract the known shorter side's square from the hypotenuse's square, then take the square root.

challenges.title: Which right angle?
challenges.prompt: To use **DE = 4e** in an equation, we need a right-angled triangle that contains DE. Which right angle do we use?
challenges.hint: D is where the diagonals cross.
challenges.explain: The diagonals meet at right angles at D, so ΔADE has a right angle at ∠ADE and contains DE.

takeaways: Pythagoras' theorem works only in **right-angled** triangles — mark every right angle in the figure first.
Split the figure into right-angled triangles and solve them **one at a time**; each answer feeds the next triangle.
Keep a few extra decimal places in the middle of a calculation and round only the **final** answer (3 s.f.).

notes.title: Exam tip
notes.text: Always begin with a line such as "In ΔABC, ∠C = 90°. Using Pythagoras' Theorem," — it shows which triangle and which right angle you are using.
